historical_timeline.summary: Born in Paris (the date on his birth certificate).
Nearly a year in the Bastille.
Falls ill with smallpox at Maisons; out of danger by 15 November.
Conducted to Calais, whence he leaves for London.
Writes that he has always had a feeble constitution.
Blood spurts from his mouth and nose after a fit of coughing; bleeding continues for several days.
Acclaimed at the Académie and crowned at a performance of Irène.
Takes a large dose of an opium preparation; strangury and catheterization in his last weeks.
Stricken with uremia, by Britannica's account.
Report of the opening of the body: diseased, thickened bladder; very large, hard prostate.
Retrospective study proposes perforated squamous cell cancer of the bladder.

claims.statement: Voltaire, the pen name of François-Marie Arouet, was born in Paris; his birth certificate gives 21 November 1694, although he stated on several occasions that he was in fact born on 20 February. He was born into a wealthy bourgeois family; his putative father, François Arouet, became a receiver in the Cour des Comptes (the audit office), and he lost his mother when he was seven. He adopted the name Voltaire in 1718.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The cause of his mother's death is not recorded in the cited sources.

claims.statement: He was imprisoned in the Bastille for nearly a year in 1717 after mocking the regent, and in May 1726, after a quarrel with the chevalier de Rohan, was beaten, taken to the Bastille, and conducted to Calais, whence he left for London.

source_links.locator: Heritage and youth; Exile to England

claims.statement: In a letter to the baron de Breteuil dated December 1723, he gave an account of the smallpox from which he was recovering: he fell ill on 4 November at Maisons; the disease declared itself after two days of fever with a slight eruption; the physician Gervasi had him take an emetic eight times and drink two hundred pints of lemonade, he had himself bled a second time on his own authority, and by the 15th he was out of danger.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own contemporary account of an illness he survived.

claims.statement: His biographer Jean Orieux, as summarized in a 1970 review in the Revue d'histoire de la pharmacie, describes a lifelong preoccupation with illness and remedies: he suffered from colic, took as many as eight purges and twelve enemas in a month, was persuaded he would die before forty, and really did suffer from his kidneys and bladder. In a letter of 1769 he wrote that being very ill was the common lot of old age, especially for one who had always had a feeble constitution.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A biographer's summary and his own words; they record digestive and urinary complaints and frequent self-medication, not a diagnosis.

claims.statement: He returned to Paris on 10 February 1778, for the first time in 28 years, to direct rehearsals of his tragedy Irène; more than 300 people called on him the day after his arrival. On 30 March he went to the Académie amid acclamations and was crowned in his box at a performance of Irène. His deteriorating health did not permit his return to Ferney.

His secretary Jean-Louis Wagnière recorded that on 25 February 1778, at a quarter past noon, while dictating from his bed, he coughed three times and said that he was spitting blood, and that blood then spurted from his mouth and nose. A declaration in his hand of 2 March 1778 states that he had been attacked for four days by a vomiting of blood, and the blood loss continued for several days.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Contemporary accounts of hemorrhage from the mouth and nose; the source of bleeding was not established. The surgeon who opened the body reported that the vessel whose rupture caused this first illness had healed.

source_links.locator: Wagnière's account and the declaration of 2 March 1778, as printed by Lachèvre

claims.statement: An anonymous and hostile manuscript account of 1778, published by Frédéric Lachèvre in 1908, claims that in May 1778, before a meeting at the Académie, he secretly took as many as eighteen cups of coffee.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A single anecdote in a hostile source; the roster's figure of 40 to 50 cups a day was not found in any source read.

source_links.locator: Anonymous manuscript, part on the Académie

claims.statement: In mid-May 1778, according to Wagnière's account, he was persuaded to take a liquor brought by an apothecary and then, in great agitation, asked the maréchal de Richelieu to send him some of his prepared opium; one witness said he saw him finish the bottle. The anonymous manuscript says he took the whole vial at once instead of dividing it into three or four doses. Orieux's account has him refuse the apothecary's remedy and accept the opium preparation brought by Richelieu, after which he felt a trail of fire from throat to bowels and became frenzied.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Several contemporary and later accounts agree that he took a large dose of an opium preparation in mid-May and differ in the details; the amount is unknown.

source_links.locator: Wagnière's account, as printed by Lachèvre, and the anonymous manuscript

claims.statement: In his last weeks he suffered from strangury and needed frequent catheterization by the surgeon Try; the anonymous manuscript describes a bladder holding as much pus as urine, which could be emptied only with a catheter, and a burning heat over the lower abdomen. Britannica records that on 18 May he was stricken with uremia and that he suffered much pain on his deathbed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Contemporary descriptions of painful urination, retention needing a catheter, and infected urine; 'uremia' is a later encyclopedia's term.

source_links.locator: Editor's introduction on the surgeon Try, and the anonymous manuscript

claims.statement: He died in Paris on 30 May 1778, aged 83, peacefully it seems, according to Britannica; his body was taken to the Abbey of Scellières and given Christian burial there, and his remains were later transferred to the Panthéon.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

claims.statement: The report of the opening and embalming of his body, dated 31 May 1778 and signed by the surgeon Try, found the brain and the organs of the chest healthy; the bladder was diseased, more than an inch thick at its upper and posterior part, with a lard-like substance and suppurating tubercles whose pus had leaked into the abdomen over the nearby intestines; the right kidney bore gangrenous marks; and the prostate was very large and entirely scirrhous. The anonymous manuscript adds that the bladder held about a pint of pus and was perforated at its base.
claims.clinical_interpretation: An eighteenth-century gross description without microscopy; 'scirrhous' meant hard.

source_links.locator: Rapport de l'ouverture et embaumement du corps, 31 May 1778, as printed by Lachèvre

claims.statement: Retrospective readings of his final illness differ. A 2025 paleoproteomic study of blood residues by Charlier and colleagues concluded that he died of a perforated squamous cell cancer of the bladder with peritoneal extension; Britannica describes uremia; the autopsy's very large, hard prostate leaves prostate disease, benign or malignant, as a further possibility.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretations; the 2025 study is known here only from its published title and bibliographic record. The record does not assert any of them as his historical diagnosis.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate visible blood in the urine with difficult urination in a frail man of 83: urinalysis with microscopy and culture, kidney function, bladder scan, and catheter drainage of chronic retention with a medication review that stops an anticholinergic sleep aid; PSA by shared decision; CT urography with chest CT and cystoscopy (AUA/SUFU); resection and staging of a muscle-invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder; a geriatric assessment and shared decision on cystectomy, trimodality therapy, and palliative hypofractionated radiotherapy matched to his goals; a febrile catheter-associated infection; and safe, low-dose opioid prescribing with naloxone in a patient with a documented opium overdose (CDC 1774, AGS Beers 1775).

assessment_plan.display: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, muscle-invasive
assessment_plan.assessment: Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the posterior wall and dome, invading muscle, with lymphovascular invasion and a mobile palpable mass under anesthesia; with the CT urography and clear chest CT, clinical stage cT3b N0 M0 (stage IIIA). Pure squamous cell carcinoma is uncommon outside regions where schistosomiasis is common; it responds less well to chemotherapy than urothelial carcinoma, and radical cystectomy offers the best chance of cure. The G8 screen is 11 of 17 (abnormal), with low weight, reduced mobility, and help needed for shopping and travel, though he is independent in self-care and thinking clearly; his creatinine is 1.22 mg/dL (eGFR 59). We discussed four paths in plain terms: radical cystectomy with an ileal conduit, with a substantial risk of complications and a long recovery at his age; daily radiotherapy over four weeks with bladder preservation; weekly palliative radiotherapy (36 Gy in six fractions) aimed at controlling bleeding and local symptoms with few visits; and symptom care alone. His goals are to stay at home, finish his play, and avoid long hospital stays, and he accepts that weekly radiotherapy is unlikely to cure the cancer

referral.question: An 83-year-old man with three weeks of visible blood in the urine with small clots, a weak stream, and chronic retention (post-void residual 460 mL) with acute kidney injury, now drained by an indwelling catheter. Please evaluate the hematuria with cystoscopy, advise on the retention and the voiding trial, and interpret his PSA
referral.urgency: Soon, within one to two weeks; the bladder is drained and he is stable
referral.pertinent_history: Voltaire is an 83-year-old writer, thin (54.2 kg, BMI 18.8) and independent in self-care, who has had visible blood in the urine for three weeks, with small clots on several days, a weak stream, straining, and frequent small voids, and has been dribbling at night. He had been taking diphenhydramine 25 mg nightly for sleep and over-the-counter sodium phosphate enemas for lifelong constipation; both were stopped today. Six weeks ago he had a large nosebleed with blood also in his mouth after a coughing fit, treated with packing in urgent care. He has never smoked and has no occupational exposure to dyes or aromatic amines. Today: bladder scan 460 mL; a 16 Fr catheter drained 520 mL of pink urine. Urine microscopy shows more than 50 red cells per high-power field and 8 white cells; culture and cytology are pending. Hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL; creatinine 1.68 mg/dL (eGFR 40), up from 1.1 a year ago; potassium 5.0 mmol/L. PSA 6.4 ng/mL, drawn before the catheter by shared decision. The prostate is enlarged, firm, and smooth without a discrete nodule. IPSS 22 before the catheter. He takes polyethylene glycol and started tamsulosin 0.4 mg today. Multiphasic CT urography with a chest CT is booked in two days. He wants to keep working on the play he is staging and to avoid long hospital stays
questions: What is the cause of the bleeding? Please perform cystoscopy and review the CT urography.
If a bladder tumor is found, what resection and staging do you advise, and what treatment options would suit a frail man of 83?
How should the retention be managed: how long should the catheter stay, and when and how should a trial without catheter be done?
How should his PSA of 6.4 ng/mL be interpreted, and is prostate MRI or biopsy warranted at his age?
Is it safe to manage the catheter and any clots at home, and what should prompt urgent return?

consultant_note.history: Voltaire is seen at the request of Dr. Delacroix-Mensah, one week after a catheter was placed for chronic retention with gross hematuria. The urine in the bag has cleared from red to light pink, with one small clot four days ago. He has had no fever, flank pain, or catheter blockage. He describes several years of a slowing stream and getting up at night, worse over the past few months, and three weeks of visible blood. He has stopped the diphenhydramine and the phosphate enemas. He has never smoked, has no exposure to aromatic amines, has not had pelvic radiation or cyclophosphamide, has not travelled where schistosomiasis is common, and has no history of bladder stones. He takes no anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug. He is frank that he would not want major surgery if it meant months of recovery
consultant_note.data_reviewed: CT urography two days after intake: 4.2 cm sessile soft-tissue mass of the posterior bladder wall extending to the dome, wall thickened to 1.8 cm with perivesical stranding; no hydronephrosis; upper tracts clear; prostate about 78 mL with a median lobe; no enlarged nodes or bone lesions. Chest CT: clear. Urine culture: no growth. Urine cytology: atypical squamous cells suspicious for malignancy. Creatinine 1.68 mg/dL at intake and 1.24 mg/dL today (eGFR 58); hemoglobin 11.6 then 11.2 g/dL; PSA 6.4 ng/mL; IPSS 22 before the catheter; post-void residual 460 mL

assessment.assessment: The bleeding comes from a solid bladder tumor whose appearance and size, with wall thickening and perivesical stranding on CT, suggest a muscle-invasive cancer; the keratinizing plaques and squamous atypia on cytology raise the possibility of squamous histology. The friable prostatic vessels may add to the bleeding. The upper tracts are clear and the chest CT shows no metastasis
Chronic high-pressure retention from prostatic obstruction, made worse by the anticholinergic sleep aid and possibly by clot and the tumor's bulk; kidney function has recovered with drainage

assessment.assessment: PSA 6.4 ng/mL with a gland of about 78 mL gives a PSA density of 0.08, low, and the gland is smooth. Retention, catheterization, and bleeding all raise the PSA. At 83, with a bladder tumor that will determine his treatment and outlook, finding a prostate cancer now would not change management, so I do not advise prostate MRI or biopsy

recommendations: Transurethral resection of the bladder tumor with examination under anesthesia in two days, resecting into muscle for diagnosis and staging; one dose of perioperative antibiotic

Keep the indwelling catheter until after the resection; then a trial without catheter on tamsulosin once he is free of infection, with a bladder scan after voiding; if he fails, intermittent self-catheterization or a long-term catheter rather than prostate surgery while the bladder cancer is treated
Continue tamsulosin; no 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor for now
No prostate MRI or biopsy, by shared decision; no further PSA testing unless it would change care

If the resection confirms muscle-invasive cancer, complete staging is already in hand with the CT urography and chest CT; a geriatric assessment should precede the treatment decision, and the options to discuss are radical cystectomy, bladder-preserving radiotherapy, weekly palliative radiotherapy, and symptom care, weighed against his goals
At home: catheter care, 1.5 to 2 liters of fluid a day, and urgent return or a call for a blocked catheter, large clots, fever, or rigors
